title: The Lake Where No Lake Should Be: Ado-Awaye's Suspended Lake

chapters.title: A Lake Where No Lake Should Be

pages.text: Water always looks for the lowest place it can find. Pour a cup of water on a slope and it runs down. Rain on a mountain becomes streams, and streams become rivers that rush downhill towards the sea. That is why most lakes lie in low places: in valleys, in hollows, and on flat plains where water gathers and stays.

So imagine climbing a great bare hill of rock in south-western Nigeria. You climb for a long time, higher and higher, above the trees and the rooftops. At the top, where you expect nothing but stone and sky, you find a lake. Still, dark green water rests quietly on the top of the hill, as if someone had carried it up there and set it down.

This lake is real. It sits above the town of Ado-Awaye in Iseyin Local Government Area, Oyo State, about twenty kilometres west of the town of Iseyin. The hill is called Oke Ado. Its long rocky ridge is sometimes called the sleeping lion, because of the shape it makes against the sky. The lake on its top is called Iyake.

image.note: Map of Nigeria with Oyo State highlighted; inset showing Iseyin and Ado-Awaye about 20 km to the west, with the Oke Ado ridge marked

pages.text: People call Iyake a suspended lake. Suspended means held up, as if hanging in the air with nothing underneath. A suspended lake, then, is a lake that seems to be held up high above the land around it. No river flows into Iyake. No stream feeds it. Its water arrives from only one place: the sky.

Iyake is not enormous. It is oval in shape and covers roughly 350 square metres, about the floor space of five classrooms put together. You could walk around its edge in a few minutes. But size is not what makes it remarkable. Plenty of lakes are bigger. Very few lakes sit where Iyake sits.

image.note: View from above: a small oval lake of still, dark green water resting in a hollow on top of a bare grey rock hill, the town and farmland far below

pages.text: That is the puzzle at the heart of this book. How can a lake stay on top of a hill, when water always runs downhill? Why does it not drain away? Where does its water come from, and how deep does it go? To answer those questions, we need to climb the hill, look closely at the rock, and listen to the people who have lived beside the lake for centuries.

The town of Ado-Awaye is old. According to the town's own history, it began around five hundred years ago, when two neighbouring communities, Ado and Awaye, joined together. Its king is called the Alado. For all that time, the hill has stood over the town, and the lake has rested on its top.

The climb begins with steps cut into the rock. Visitors describe hundreds of them, though the counts differ from one report to the next. The steps are rough and uneven, worn smooth in places by countless feet. After the steps, the path crosses bare rock and patches of trees. Guides advise visitors to wear proper shoes, carry plenty of water, and take their time.

image.note: Rough steps cut into a steep grey rock face, a local guide leading a small group of climbers upward, trees and the town visible below

pages.text: The hill is full of things to notice on the way up. Some are natural, like the fallen tree whose twisted shape looks so much like an elephant that everyone calls it the Elephant Tree. Some were shaped by people long ago. And some carry stories that the people of Ado-Awaye have told for generations. The hill is a kind of museum without walls.

One of the first sights is Ishage Rock, a great boulder perched on the hillside. Local people regard it as a rain rock. It is said that when the land needs rain, a priest wraps the lower part of the rock in white cloth. To the community, Ishage is not simply a stone. It is part of how they understand the weather and the land.

image.note: A large rounded boulder on the hillside, its lower half wrapped in white cloth, under a cloudy sky

pages.text: Further on, small round holes are scattered across the rock surface. They are called Ese Awon Agba, the footprints of the elders. Local tradition says they were left by ancestors who walked here long ago. Historians have another explanation. They think the hollows were worn into the rock by people grinding grain and other materials in the same spots, over many years.

Both explanations tell us something. The historians' idea tells us that people lived and worked on this hill for a very long time. The traditional story tells us how much the hill matters to the people below it. A careful reader can hold both at once: what the evidence shows, and what a place means to the people who belong to it.

chapters.title: How Can a Lake Sit on a Hill?

pages.text: To understand Iyake, start with the rock. South-western Nigeria is dotted with great domes and ridges of very old, very hard rock that rise sharply out of the flatter land around them. Olumo Rock in Abeokuta is one famous example. Oke Ado is another. Rock like this has been slowly worn down by sun, wind and rain for an extremely long time.

image.note: Cross-section diagram of the hill: hard rock dome, a bowl-shaped hollow at the top filled with rainwater, arrows showing rain falling and running into the hollow

pages.text: Wearing away does not happen evenly. Softer or more cracked parts of the rock break down faster than the harder parts. Over enormous stretches of time, this uneven wearing can carve out a hollow: a dip in the surface of the rock, shaped like a bowl. Scientists think this is how the basin that holds Iyake was formed.

Now add rain. South-western Nigeria has a long rainy season, lasting from around March or April until October. Rain falls on the hilltop, runs across the bare rock, and collects in the lowest place it can find. On top of Oke Ado, the lowest place is the bowl. The water gathers there, and the bowl becomes a lake.

Why does the water not simply soak away? Hard, solid rock lets very little water pass through it. Soil drinks rain like a sponge, but a bowl of solid rock behaves more like a basin in a kitchen. Some water may escape slowly through cracks, and some rises back into the air as the sun warms it, but much of it stays where it has fallen.

People who live near the lake say something even more surprising: that its level hardly changes. They say it does not dry up in the dry season and does not overflow in the rains. No one has yet fully explained why. One possible reason is that cracks in the rock let extra water drain away when the lake is full. But that is an idea still to be tested, not a proven fact.

Then there is the question of depth. Visitors are often told the lake is bottomless. In truth, no one has measured how deep it is. The water is dark, entering it is forbidden, and the hollow beneath could be shallow or quite deep. Bottomless is a story. Unknown is the honest answer, and unknown is exactly what makes scientists curious.

For the people of Ado-Awaye, Iyake is far more than a curiosity. It is sacred. The lake has been at the centre of the town's beliefs and ceremonies for generations, and traditional rites are still held there. To visit Iyake is to visit a holy place, and visitors are expected to behave with care and respect.

The name Iyake is often explained as meaning a woman's cry. It comes from an old story. A woman, it is said, longed with all her heart for a child. Her sorrow was so deep that she turned into water, and the water became the lake. Some say her cry can still be heard in the wind that moves across its surface.

image.note: A woman in traditional Yoruba dress sitting quietly at the edge of the lake at dusk, looking out over the still water; calm, gentle mood

pages.text: Because of that story, many people believe the lake has a special power to help women who wish to have children. Others believe its water can heal illness, and some carry a little of it home. Whatever a visitor believes, these beliefs show how closely the lake is woven into the hopes and lives of the community.

There are strict rules. No one may swim in Iyake or wade into it. Near the lake is a small hole known as Agbomofunyake. Tradition warns that anyone who puts a foot in it when it is full of water will be pulled down into the lake and never return. Many people speak quietly near the water's edge, as they would in a place of worship.

It is worth noticing that the rules protect people as well as the lake. The water is dark, the edges are rock, and the depth is unknown. A lake like that can be dangerous. A community that forbids swimming keeps its children safe, and it also keeps the lake clean and undisturbed. Respect and good sense point the same way.

The lake brings people together too. Festivals are held on the hill, and the Oyo State Government has set up a festival in the lake's name to welcome visitors. The Alado and the people of Ado-Awaye hope that more Nigerians, and visitors from around the world, will make the climb, as long as they treat the hill with respect.

image.note: Families and visitors gathered on the rocky hilltop during a festival, colourful clothing, drummers, the lake visible behind them at a respectful distance

pages.text: You will often hear that Iyake is one of only two suspended lakes in the world. The other one usually named is Hanging Lake, in Glenwood Canyon in the state of Colorado, in the United States. Comparing the two is a good way to see what makes Iyake special, and also a good way to practise thinking carefully about big claims.

Hanging Lake formed when a fault, a crack in the earth's crust, caused a section of the valley floor to drop. A waterfall tumbles into it from a creek above, and minerals carried in that water have slowly built up its rocky edges. It is beautiful, but it is fed by flowing water. Iyake has no stream and no waterfall. It is fed by rain alone.

image.note: Side-by-side comparison: left, Hanging Lake in a green canyon with a waterfall pouring into clear turquoise water; right, Iyake on a bare rock hilltop with rain clouds above and no stream

pages.text: So is Iyake truly one of only two? That depends on what you count. Around the world there are many lakes high in mountains, and some sit in the craters of old volcanoes. Whether those count as suspended lakes is a question of definition. Good thinkers notice when a claim depends on how a word is defined, and ask exactly what is being compared.

What experts do agree on is that Iyake is precious. In 2024, the Ado-Awaye Suspended Lake was named a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention, a worldwide agreement to protect important wetlands. The Ramsar listing describes it as the only mountaintop suspended lake in Africa. That is a remarkable title for a lake the size of a few classrooms.

image.note: The lake on its hilltop in morning light, a small group of visitors standing well back from the edge, the town spread out far below

pages.text: Protection matters because places like this are fragile. Litter, careless visitors, and damage to the plants and rock around the lake could harm it. A wetland on a hilltop also does useful work: it stores rainwater and releases it slowly, which helps the land below. Looking after Iyake means looking after the whole hill and the community around it.

Water runs downhill. Every child learns that, and it is true. But on top of a rock in Oyo State, rain has gathered in a bowl of stone for longer than anyone can remember, making a lake where no lake should be. Science can explain part of its story. The people of Ado-Awaye hold the rest. Both are worth the climb.
